articles.title: The Man Who Carried the Rope
articles.dek: On a stormy night in 1859, one sailor swam a line through the surf so others could follow. Hebrews 6 says Jesus did the same for every soul still waiting on a promise.
articles.quote: Your hope holds because Jesus went ahead of you through the storm and tied the line to solid ground.
articles.body:
On the night of October 25, 1859, a steam clipper called the Royal Charter was almost home. She had sailed from Melbourne with close to five hundred people aboard, many of them miners coming back from the Australian goldfields with their savings sewn into belts and coats. Off the coast of Anglesey in north Wales, within a day of Liverpool, a storm of hurricane strength came howling out of the north and drove her toward the rocks near the village of Moelfre. The crew let go both anchors and fought through the dark hours, but before dawn the chains parted and the ship struck the rocks only a few yards from shore.

Those few yards were a wall of white water. Passengers could see land from the deck, and villagers had gathered on the rocks with lanterns, but the surf between them would have smashed anyone who tried to cross. Then a seaman from Malta named Joseph Rodgers (he was born Guzeppi Ruggier) offered to do what everyone else feared. He tied a rope around his body, went over the side, and battled through the breakers toward the rocks, where men on shore dragged him out half-drowned. The line he carried was made fast, a heavier hawser was pulled across after it, and a bosun’s chair was rigged so that people could be hauled from the wreck to the land.

The storm still claimed most of the ship that night, and the loss is remembered as one of the worst in Welsh history. Yet about forty people lived, and several of them came ashore along the rope Rodgers had carried through the sea. He was later honored by the Royal National Lifeboat Institution, and Moelfre has kept his name. His courage was simple and physical: he went first into the place everyone dreaded, so that a line would run from a breaking ship to solid ground.

That picture of one person going ahead with a line sits close to the heart of Hebrews 6. The letter was written to Jewish believers in Jesus who were tired. They had endured public insult, prison, and the confiscation of their property (Hebrews 10:32–34), and some were tempted to slip back into older, safer ways of faith. Chapter 6 opens with one of the sternest warnings in the New Testament, about those who taste the goodness of God and then turn away (6:4–6). Then the writer’s voice softens into something close to an embrace: “Even though we speak like this, dear friends, we are convinced of better things in your case” (6:9).

To steady these weary people, the writer reaches back two thousand years to Abraham. God had promised a childless man in his seventies a son and descendants as many as the stars. Then came the waiting, through years of living in tents and moving from pasture to pasture, through Sarah’s bitter laugh and Abraham’s own anxious shortcuts, through long seasons when heaven seemed silent. When Isaac finally arrived, God asked Abraham to lay that very son on an altar on Mount Moriah. After Abraham obeyed and the boy was spared, God spoke again: “I swear by myself, declares the LORD, that because you have done this… I will surely bless you” (Genesis 22:16–17).

Hebrews lingers over that moment. “When God made his promise to Abraham, since there was no one greater for him to swear by, he swore by himself” (6:13). The writer explains that “people swear by someone greater than themselves, and the oath confirms what is said and puts an end to all argument” (6:16). In the ancient world you swore by your king or your gods, something higher than you that would punish you if you lied. God had nothing higher to appeal to, so he put his own name and character on the table. “And so after waiting patiently, Abraham received what was promised” (6:15). The Greek word behind “waiting patiently” is makrothymēsas, which literally pictures a long breath or a long temper, the steadiness of a person who does not snap when the promise is slow in coming.

Then the writer turns the oath toward the reader. “Because God wanted to make the unchanging nature of his purpose very clear to the heirs of what was promised, he confirmed it with an oath. God did this so that, by two unchangeable things in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us may be greatly encouraged” (6:17–18). The two unchangeable things are God’s promise and God’s oath. His word alone was always enough, and he added the oath as a kindness to people who find it hard to believe. The phrase “fled to take hold” uses the verb katapheugō, and many scholars hear in it an echo of the cities of refuge in Israel, where a person in danger could run and be safe (Deuteronomy 19:5). Hope, in this picture, is a place you run to when the storm is behind you.

“We have this hope as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure. It enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain, where our forerunner, Jesus, has entered on our behalf. He has become a high priest forever, in the order of Melchizedek.” (Hebrews 6:19–20)

Every sailor knows that an anchor drops down into the dark water below. The writer of Hebrews pictures this anchor going in a surprising direction, up and inward, into “the inner sanctuary behind the curtain.” For a Jewish reader those words meant the Most Holy Place, the innermost room of the tabernacle, where God’s presence dwelt and where the high priest entered only once a year on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). The hope of a believer is fastened in the very presence of God, in the one room on earth that ordinary people were never allowed to see.

The word that opens the passage most is “forerunner,” prodromos in Greek. It described a scout or an advance runner, someone sent ahead so that others could come after. No high priest in Israel was ever called a forerunner. He went behind the curtain alone, on behalf of the people, and then he came back out, and nobody followed him in. Jesus entered “on our behalf” as the first of a great company, the one who goes ahead so that the rest can come. Later the same letter says that he opened for us “a new and living way… through the curtain” (Hebrews 10:20). Like Joseph Rodgers in the surf at Moelfre, he went first through the place we could never cross, and he made the line fast on the other side. Your hope holds because Jesus went ahead of you through the storm and tied the line to solid ground.

This matters most in the long middle of waiting, which is where Abraham lived for decades and where many of us live now. Perhaps you are waiting for a child to come home to faith, for a diagnosis to change, for a job abroad to end so the family can finally sit at one table. In a week when Super Typhoon Rosal has only just left Philippine waters, families in Batanes and northern Luzon understand very well what it means to hold on through a long night and wait for the wind to drop. The waiting is real, and Hebrews never pretends otherwise. It simply tells you where the other end of your rope is tied.

One practical way to live this today is to name the promise you are holding and say it back to God with Hebrews 6:18 in mind, reminding your own heart that he has given both his word and his oath. When fear rises, move one hand along the rope instead of looking at the waves: a verse read in the morning, a short prayer at noon, a word of thanks before you sleep. The writer also reminds weary believers that “God is not unjust; he will not forget your work and the love you have shown him as you have helped his people” (6:10). The quiet faithfulness you offer while you wait is seen and remembered.

The survivors of the Royal Charter did not have to swim the surf themselves. They had to trust the line and keep their grip while they were carried across. That is the invitation of Hebrews 6 for you this Friday. The One who swore by himself has already gone ahead, the rope is fastened in the presence of God, and every hand you place on it today brings you a little nearer to the shore.

articles.title: No One to Comfort Her
articles.dek: Five times in one chapter, a ruined city cries that nobody has come to sit with her. The cry still matters, and so does the answer God eventually gave.
articles.quote: Comfort was never meant to be a prize for people who suffered blamelessly; it is the bread God hands to the broken, whatever broke them.
articles.body:
In December 1862, Abraham Lincoln was carrying more weight than anyone in America. On December 13 the Union army had been cut down at Fredericksburg, where brigade after brigade marched toward a stone wall on Marye's Heights and fell in rows. His cabinet was quarreling, the newspapers were merciless, and the final text of the Emancipation Proclamation, which he would sign on New Year's Day, was still being worked over on his desk. Yet on December 23, with all of that pressing on him, the President took a sheet of paper and wrote to a young woman in Bloomington, Illinois, named Fanny McCullough.

Fanny's father, Lieutenant Colonel William McCullough, was an old friend from Lincoln's years as a traveling lawyer in Illinois. He had been killed earlier that month leading a night charge in Mississippi, and word reached Washington that his daughter was sinking under her grief. Lincoln knew that country well, because ten months earlier he had buried his own eleven-year-old son, Willie. So he wrote to her plainly, as one mourner to another: "Perfect relief is not possible, except with time. You can not now realize that you will ever feel better. Is not this so? And yet it is a mistake. You are sure to be happy again." He signed it simply, "Your sincere friend, A. Lincoln." Fanny kept that letter for the rest of her life, and it survives today.

The words are lovely, but what carried them to her was the fact that a busy, grieving man stopped and came near. That small act of nearness is exactly what a forgotten book of the Bible says a broken person needs most, and it is the very thing the speaker in Lamentations could not find.

Lamentations was written in the smoke of the worst disaster in Israel's history. In 586 BC the Babylonian army of Nebuchadnezzar broke through Jerusalem's walls after a long, starving siege. They burned Solomon's temple, tore down the city, and marched thousands of its people into exile. Jewish and Christian tradition has long linked the book with the prophet Jeremiah, who lived through those days, though the poems themselves do not name their author. Whoever he was, he stood among the ashes and wrote.

The book opens with a single Hebrew word, 'ekah, which means "How!" It is the gasp of someone who cannot believe what he is seeing, and Jewish readers still call the whole book by that name. "How deserted lies the city, once so full of people! How like a widow is she, who once was great among the nations!" (Lamentations 1:1). The poet then does something tender and daring. He stops describing Jerusalem as a place and begins speaking of her as a woman, a widow sitting alone at night with tears on her cheeks (1:2). Halfway through the chapter she finds her own voice and begins to speak for herself.

The poem is built with great care. Each of its twenty-two verses begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, from aleph to taw, as if the poet wanted to grieve the whole loss from A to Z and leave nothing unsaid. Through that orderly alphabet a single phrase keeps returning like a toll of a bell. "Among all her lovers there is no one to comfort her" (1:2). "There was none to comfort her" (1:9). "Zion stretches out her hands, but there is no one to comfort her" (1:17). "People have heard my groaning, but there is no one to comfort me" (1:21). And at the center of it all, the widow herself says:

"This is why I weep and my eyes overflow with tears. No one is near to comfort me, no one to restore my spirit." (Lamentations 1:16)

The Hebrew word behind "comfort" is menachem, from the verb nacham, which carries the sense of drawing a deep breath, of easing someone's heaviness so they can breathe again. A menachem is a person who does that for you. Jerusalem had lost her temple, her king, and her children, yet the loss she names again and again is the absence of that one person. The "lovers" of verse 2 were the allied nations she had trusted instead of God, and they had all walked away.

Here the chapter becomes uncomfortable in a way that turns out to be a gift. Lamentations is honest that Jerusalem's ruin was largely her own doing. "Jerusalem has sinned greatly" (1:8), the poet admits, and the widow herself confesses, "The LORD is righteous, yet I rebelled against his command" (1:18). The opening verses of chapter 2 go further still, describing the Lord himself throwing down the strongholds and even rejecting his own altar (2:1–7). By any human reckoning this was a city reaping what she had sown.

And still the poem treats the lack of a comforter as a real wound. One way to read this is that Scripture refuses to make comfort something a person has to earn. Most of us quietly ration our sympathy by merit. We rush to the family whose house burned in a typhoon, and we hesitate at the door of the cousin buried in debt from his own gambling, the friend whose marriage collapsed because of her own choices, or the relative who ignored every warning. We tell ourselves they need a lecture first. Lamentations sits in the ashes with a guilty city and says she needs someone near.

God's own answer came later, and it is one of the most beautiful echoes in the Bible. Many scholars have observed that the second half of Isaiah speaks back to Lamentations, line by line. The book that cried "no one to comfort her" is met by the words, "Comfort, comfort my people, says your God. Speak tenderly to Jerusalem" (Isaiah 40:1–2). The Hebrew is nachamu, nachamu, the same root doubled, spoken to the very same city that had sinned. A few chapters later God goes further: "I, even I, am he who comforts you" (Isaiah 51:12). The empty chair beside the widow was finally taken by the Lord himself. Jesus carried the same promise forward when he said, "Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted" (Matthew 5:4). Comfort was never meant to be a prize for people who suffered blamelessly; it is the bread God hands to the broken, whatever broke them.

Paul then shows us where that comfort is meant to go next. God "comforts us in all our troubles, so that we can comfort those in any trouble with the comfort we ourselves receive from God" (2 Corinthians 1:4). The comfort you have received is meant to pass through your hands into someone else's. That is what Lincoln did with his grief over Willie: he turned his own sorrow into a letter that a young woman could hold.

Filipinos already understand this better than most. At a lamay, people come and stay through the night. They bring food, they sit on borrowed monobloc chairs, they keep the family company until morning. Few of them say anything profound, and that is perfectly fine, because their presence is the message. The widow in Lamentations would have given anything for one such visitor, and very likely someone in your life feels the same way tonight, especially someone whose trouble is partly their own fault and who assumes everyone has walked away.

You do not need perfect words to be that person. Lincoln himself admitted that "perfect relief is not possible," and he wrote anyway. Today you might think of the one name that has crossed your mind more than once lately, the person you have been avoiding because their situation is messy or because you are unsure what to say, and send them a short message, make a call, or knock on their door with a bag of pandesal. Let them breathe a little easier for an hour.

If you are the one sitting alone in the ruins right now, even ruins you helped build, hear the answer God gave Jerusalem. He did not leave her chair empty forever, and he will not leave yours empty either. "I, even I, am he who comforts you." You are sure, as Lincoln told Fanny, to be happy again.

articles.title: Room Inside the Rings
articles.dek: A hunted man in Psalm 119 says God's commands are what set him free. A stalk of kawayan bending in a typhoon shows how he could mean it.
articles.quote: God's commands are the rings in the bamboo, the places that hold your shape when the wind comes, so that you can keep rising into open sky.
articles.body:
After a typhoon crosses northern Luzon, you can drive past fields where mango trees lie on their sides and acacias have lost whole limbs. Along the riverbanks, though, the clumps of kawayan are usually still standing. They bowed all night, sometimes low enough for their tops to brush the mud, and by morning they had lifted themselves upright again. Our grandparents pointed to the bamboo and told us to be like it, humble enough to bend and strong enough to rise.

Few of us were ever told why bamboo can do this. Split a stalk lengthwise and you find it is hollow, which ought to make it weak, because a long hollow tube under strain usually kinks and folds like a drinking straw. At every node, the ring you see on the outside, the hollow is closed off by a solid wall of tissue called a diaphragm. Engineers who study bamboo have found that these walls keep the tube round as it bends, so it can flex without collapsing. They also stop cracks. A split that begins in one section of the stalk tends to halt when it reaches the next node, so the damage stays in one segment instead of running the whole length. The partitions that seem to block the open space inside are what allow the plant to grow tall and stay standing once the wind arrives.

I thought of the kawayan this week while reading a stanza from the longest chapter in the Bible. In it, a man under pressure says that God's commands are the reason he is free, which most of us would not expect.

Psalm 119 is an acrostic, a poem built on the Hebrew alphabet. It works through all twenty-two letters, gives each letter eight verses, and begins every verse in a stanza with that stanza's letter. Today's section, verses 41 to 48, belongs to the letter vav. Very few Hebrew words begin with vav, and the most common is the small word for “and.” So the poet did something tender: nearly every line in this stanza begins, in Hebrew, with “and.” Read that way, it sounds like a man adding one hope to the next, the way a child keeps lengthening a prayer at bedtime because there is always one more thing to tell the Father.

We do not know his name, but the psalm tells us his situation. He is being taunted (verse 42). Proud people have smeared him with lies (verse 69), and rulers have sat together and spoken against him (verse 23). He is a man with very little room. He opens the stanza with a request: “May your unfailing love come to me, LORD, your salvation, according to your promise” (Psalm 119:41). The Hebrew word behind “unfailing love” is chesed, God's loyal, covenant-keeping kindness, the love that keeps its promises long after ordinary affection would have given up. He asks for that love first, and only afterward does he speak about obeying. Then, in the middle of the stanza, he makes his surprising claim.

“I will walk about in freedom, for I have sought out your precepts.” (Psalm 119:45)

The phrase translated “in freedom” is barechavah, which literally means “in a wide place.” Its root, rachav, describes something broad and spacious. Isaac used that root when, after a long string of quarrels over wells, he finally dug one that nobody fought him for and named it Rehoboth, saying, “Now the LORD has given us room and we will flourish in the land” (Genesis 26:22). David used it when he sang, “He brought me out into a spacious place; he rescued me because he delighted in me” (Psalm 18:19). In the Hebrew imagination, trouble is a tight place. The word often translated “distress,” tsar, carries the picture of being squeezed. Salvation is room to breathe.

So a man hemmed in by mockers says that the precepts of God have given him room. One way to read this is that God's word works in a life the way the nodes work in a stalk of bamboo. From a distance each command can look like a wall set across the open hollow of our own wishes. When the pressure comes, those same walls hold our shape. A harsh word spoken at work can stay at work because you have already settled, before God, that you will not carry it home and pour it on your children. A temptation that opens in one lonely season meets a place where your answer was decided long ago, and the crack goes no further. A life without those inner walls may look more open, but it tends to buckle at the first strong wind.

The verb in verse 45 also matters. “Sought out” translates darash, a word used for searching, inquiring, and going after something on purpose. The psalmist did more than tolerate God's rules. He went looking for them, the way a farmer walks his land looking for where the water runs. Three verses later he goes further: “I reach out for your commands, which I love, that I may meditate on your decrees” (Psalm 119:48). The Hebrew reads, “I lift up my hands to your commands,” the same posture of prayer and worship found in Psalm 134:2. He loves God's word so much that he greets it with raised hands.

The order of the stanza explains how anyone could feel that way. It begins with God's unfailing love coming toward the psalmist (verse 41), and it ends with the psalmist's love reaching back toward God's commands (verses 47 and 48). Obedience sits in between, held on both sides by love. A command received from someone who has already rescued you feels very different from a rule handed down by a stranger. James saw the same thing centuries later when he called God's word “the perfect law that gives freedom” (James 1:25). The law is the same; the heart receiving it has been changed by grace.

Look also at where the freedom leads. A man with no room says, “I will speak of your statutes before kings and will not be put to shame” (Psalm 119:46). The one who started the stanza being taunted finishes it standing in throne rooms with nothing to hide. That is what the wide place looks like in practice: a person at peace in their own conscience can walk into any room, including rooms full of powerful people who look down on them.

Many of us feel squeezed right now. Perhaps the money does not stretch to the end of the month, or you are working abroad and carrying the hopes of a whole family on one salary, or there is a relationship at home that leaves you tired before the day begins. In seasons like these, God's commands can start to feel like one more weight. The psalmist would gently suggest the opposite order. Begin where he began, by asking for God's chesed to come to you today, according to his promise. Then choose one command you have been treating as a fence, perhaps “Do not let the sun go down while you are still angry” (Ephesians 4:26), or the call to rest one day in seven, and ask the Lord tonight to show you the room it is trying to make in your life.

The next time you pass a stand of kawayan, look at the rings along the stalk. Each one marks a place where the plant was sealed and strengthened so that it could keep growing upward. God's commands are the rings in the bamboo, the places that hold your shape when the wind comes, so that you can keep rising into open sky. The storm may bend you low tonight, and his love, which came to you first, will lift you upright by morning.

articles.title: The Name Worth a Hundred Million Dollars
articles.dek: In 1982 one company spent a fortune to keep its good name. Proverbs 22 calls a good name worth more than riches. The gospel tells us what to do when our own name is already damaged.
articles.quote: Burke spent a fortune to protect a good name; Jesus spent his own good name to give us one.
articles.body:
In the autumn of 1982, seven people in the Chicago area died after taking Extra-Strength Tylenol capsules that someone had laced with cyanide. The poison had been slipped into bottles after they reached store shelves, and investigators soon confirmed that the factories were clean. Even so, the chairman of Johnson & Johnson, a soft-spoken man named James Burke, faced a question no business school had prepared him for. What should a company do when the product carrying its name has become, through no fault of its own, a source of fear in medicine cabinets across an entire country?

There were voices urging a smaller, more careful response, since a nationwide recall would be ruinously expensive. Burke turned instead to a single page his company had kept since 1943, a credo written by Robert Wood Johnson. It said the company’s first responsibility was to the doctors, nurses, patients, mothers and fathers who used its products, and it listed the shareholders last. With that page as his guide, Burke pulled roughly 31 million bottles off shelves at a cost of about $100 million, offered to exchange capsules for tablets free of charge, and spoke openly to the public about what the company knew and what it was still trying to learn.

Within weeks Tylenol’s share of the painkiller market fell from about 35 percent to single digits. Within a year, relaunched in the triple-sealed, tamper-resistant packaging we now take for granted on nearly everything we swallow, it had won most of that share back. Business schools still teach the case as the model of crisis leadership, and Burke spoke afterward about how much that old credo had steadied him when the pressure was greatest. The company lost a great deal of money, and in exchange the public concluded that the name on the bottle could be trusted.

King Solomon would have understood Burke’s choice immediately. Proverbs 22 falls near the end of the longest collection in the book, the “proverbs of Solomon” that begins at 10:1 and runs to 22:16. These are short, two-line sayings, gathered largely to train young people in Israel for the responsibilities of household, market and court. They read like a father’s advice written down so it would outlive him, and this chapter opens with a saying that any merchant weighing silver on a balance in the markets of Jerusalem would have felt as a direct challenge.

“A good name is more desirable than great riches; to be esteemed is better than silver or gold.” (Proverbs 22:1, NIV)

The Hebrew word for “name” is shem, and it carries more weight than our English word does. In the Old Testament a person’s name stands for the whole person as others come to know them, their character and their reputation together. When Scripture speaks of God’s name, it means God himself as he has revealed himself to his people. So a “good name” here means a life whose character has become trustworthy in the eyes of everyone who deals with it.

The phrase “more desirable” translates nibchar, from the verb bachar, “to choose.” Read literally, the line says a good name is to be chosen over great riches. Solomon frames reputation as a decision, and usually the decision comes at a moment when the money and the name pull in opposite directions, as they did in Burke’s office in 1982. The second line deepens it further. “To be esteemed” renders the Hebrew chen tov, “good favor,” and chen is the Old Testament’s word for grace. It is the same word in Genesis 6:8: “But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.” One way to read the verse, then, is as a movement from what we choose to what we receive. We choose integrity, and favor comes to us as a gift.

The verses that follow keep that balance. “Rich and poor have this in common: The LORD is the Maker of them all” (Proverbs 22:2), which means a good name is open to the jeepney driver and the company president alike, since both answer to the same Maker. “Humility is the fear of the LORD; its wages are riches and honor and life” (Proverbs 22:4). Then the passage closes with a word to parents: “Start children off on the way they should go, and even when they are old they will not turn from it” (Proverbs 22:6). Solomon seems to be saying that a good name is built in the home long before it is tested in public, the way Johnson & Johnson’s credo was written thirty-nine years before the crisis that proved it.

Many Filipinos grew up hearing a version of this from a parent or a lola: “Huwag mong sirain ang pangalan ng pamilya.” Don’t ruin the family name. The warning is wise, and it also leaves an honest reader with a hard question. What if the name is already damaged? Some of us carry debts we never repaid, words we cannot take back, or a family story the barangay still remembers. Proverbs tells us to choose a good name, yet for many people the choosing feels like it ended years ago.

This is where the gospel meets the proverb. Paul writes that Christ Jesus, though he was in very nature God, “made himself nothing by taking the very nature of a servant” (Philippians 2:7). The older King James Version translates that phrase as “made himself of no reputation,” which captures the sense well. The Son of God let his own good name be dragged through the dust. His critics called him “a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (Matthew 11:19), and he died the death reserved for criminals, outside the city walls. Burke spent a fortune to protect a good name; Jesus spent his own good name to give us one.

Paul continues, “Therefore God exalted him to the highest place and gave him the name that is above every name” (Philippians 2:9). Those who trust Christ are brought under that name. Believers are baptized “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19), and in Antioch the early disciples were first called by it: “The disciples were called Christians first at Antioch” (Acts 11:26). The chen of Proverbs 22:1, the favor we could never purchase with silver or gold, is given freely to people whose own names were spent. Your reputation in the eyes of God rests on Christ’s record, and that record cannot be tampered with.

Once that is settled, choosing a good name each day becomes an act of gratitude instead of an anxious effort to repair the past. The choosing happens in ordinary places, such as returning the extra change the cashier handed you by mistake, or calling a client to explain a delay before they discover it on their own. Burke had his decision mostly made for him by a page written decades earlier, and you can do something similar. Before today ends, write one or two sentences describing what you want your name to mean to the people who deal with you, and keep it where you will see it when money and integrity begin to pull apart. If you are a parent, read it aloud at the dinner table, since children learn a family’s credo mostly by watching whether the adults keep it.

A good name is worth far more than the hundred million dollars Johnson & Johnson spent to keep its own, and the good news of the gospel is that the best name of all has already been paid for. You carry it into the market, the office and the kitchen today as a gift from the One whose name is above every name. Live under it gladly, choose well in the small moments, and trust that the favor Solomon spoke of rests on you already through Christ.
